study.title: Isaiah 62 The Restoration of Zion, the watchfulness of prayer, and the arrival of salvation
study.overview: Isaiah 62 presents a promise of restoration to Zion/ Jerusalem in the language of honor, covenant, and joy. The chapter begins with the determination not to be silent until the justice and salvation of Jerusalem becomes visible to the nations. Then God renames the city, described as beloved, married and guarded, and summons sentinels and intercessors to persevere until the divine purpose is fulfilled. Finally, the text announces a road prepared for the people and proclaims the arrival of salvation with reward, culminating in the identity of "povo santo" and "unforsaken city."

outline.title: The righteousness of Zion made visible
outline.explanation: The prophet declares that his proclamation will not cease until Jerusalem shines with justice and salvation. The glory of Zion is not presented as mere material reconstruction, but as a transformation recognized by the nations, which will see the honor given by God and a new name imposed by the mouth of the LORD. The image of crown and diadema communicates value, belonging, and distinction in the eyes of God.

outline.title: New Name, Love Alliance and Persevering Vigilance
outline.explanation: The city that could once be seen as abandoned is called a grace and married one, because the LORD is delighted in it. Marriage language depicts an intimate and joyful covenant relationship. Then God establishes guards and calls upon them not to silence themselves, insisting on prayer and intercession until Jerusalem is placed as praise on earth. The divine oath ensures that enemies will no longer consume the fruit of the work of the people, and those who gather the harvest will enjoy it before the sanctuary.

outline.title: Prepare the way and announce the salvation that comes
outline.explanation: The scene changes to a public call: it is necessary to prepare the way, remove obstacles and raise a flag for the people. The announcement runs to the ends of the earth: the salvation of Zion is accompanied by reward and payment. The final result is identity and community: the people are called a holy, redeemed from the LORD, and the city receives a name that affirms its search and its permanence in the hands of God.

study.context: The chapter is presented as a continuity of the promises of restoration already announced in the book, resuming themes that the notes relate to the return of the people and to the public manifestation of the saving action of God. The notes connect the text to the consolation after exile and the expectation of a restored people, without requiring historical details beyond that. There is also strong liturgical and prophetic language: proclamation, watch, prayer, divine oath and proclamation to nations.
study.theology: Isaiah 62 emphasizes that the restoration of God's people is born from the divine initiative and becomes visible in righteousness, holiness and joy of covenant. The identity of Zion is redefined by God: what was abandonment becomes delight; what was desolation becomes marriage; what was shame becomes crown. The text also shows that God's promise does not eliminate prayer, but requires it: the sentinels must persevere without silence until fulfillment. Theologically, salvation is public, community and recognizable by the nations. Holiness is not ancillary; it is part of the fate of the redeemed people. The images of reward, harvest and sanctuary indicate that God not only rescues, but also establishes communion, stability and joy of worship.

scholarViews.insight: The true beauty of God's people is not in material riches or in a rebuilt city, but in its righteousness, which will become visible to others and attractive to the nations.
The prophet and the guards of the city represent the continual call to preaching and prayer; God orthieseths and intercession until Jerusalem is established as praise on earth.
The new name and the language of marriage portray restoration as a change of status and relationship: a previously desolate city comes to be seen as graced, sought and redeemed.

questions: How does my life make visible the righteousness of God rather than just an external religious appearance?
In which areas have I silent when the text calls perseverance in prayer and proclamation without rest?
How does the image of God like the one who rejoices with his people confronts my vision of discipline, restoration and belonging?
study.practice: Take time to intercede for your church and the work of God until there are visible fruits of righteousness, holiness and witness. Also review your way of speaking about the community of faith: instead of describing it for needs or defeats, learn to confess what God promises to do in it. Finally, practice active hope: remove concrete obstacles to serve, witness and worship, as one who prepares the way for the coming of God's salvation.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the emphasis on restoration, covenant, prayer and proclamation, but do not authorize precise historical details beyond the general reference to exile and return. The reading of Adam Clarke that associates the "new name" to "Christian" should be treated as an interpretation of it, not as a single and definitive sense of the verse. It is also not possible, from the notes alone, to determine conclusively to what extent some expressions are fulfilled exclusively in the return of exile, in the community of later faith or at both levels.
